title: When teams change architecture
summary: Read two cases of an architecture change and say what drove the choice and when it would not apply.
learningObjectives: Find the constraint behind a decision
Judge when a case does not transfer
keyTakeaways: Every case had constraints you may not share
Do not copy a famous company's choice
explanation:
When reading any case, ask three questions: **what constraint forced the choice**, **what did they give up**, and **what would have to be true for you to do the same**.

The cases below are SAMPLE scenarios for testing the layout. They are labelled illustrative on purpose.

blocks.title: A small shop keeps its monolith
blocks.situation: A six-person team runs one application and feels pressure to split it into services.
blocks.choice: They keep the single application and add module boundaries inside it.
reasons: No part of the app scales differently from the rest
blocks.outcome: Deploys stay simple and the team ships features faster.
blocks.lesson: Split a system when teams or scaling needs differ, not because services are fashionable.

blocks.title: A busy product splits its search
blocks.situation: Search traffic is far heavier than the rest of the app and slows everything during peaks.
blocks.choice: They move search to its own service with its own scaling.
reasons: Search load is spiky and different from other load
blocks.outcome: Peaks no longer slow checkout, at the price of extra operational work.
blocks.lesson: Extract a part when its load or ownership genuinely differs, and accept the operational cost.

commonMistakes: Ignoring that their team size and traffic were different

quiz.question: What drove the monolith case?
quiz.explanation: With one team and uniform load there was no reason to split.

quiz.question: In the search case, which change would make splitting unnecessary?
options: Search load becomes similar to the rest
quiz.explanation: The split was driven by uneven load; remove that and the reason goes.

quiz.question: What is NOT safe to conclude from either case?
options: Every company should copy one of them
Keeping a monolith can be fine
quiz.explanation: Cases show reasoning under specific constraints, not a universal answer.

recommendedResources.title: Martin Fowler: MonolithFirst
recommendedResources.whyRecommended: A well-known essay on when to split a system.

socraticChallenge.scenario: Your team of 4 reads that a large company split into 200 services.
socraticChallenge.question: Should you?
socraticChallenge.idealAnswer: Probably not: your constraints (team size, load) differ. Ask what drove their split and whether the same driver exists for you.

exercises.prompt: Your app has one team but one component has 10x the load. What do you do?
exercises.answer: Consider extracting just that component, since the load differs, and keep the rest together to limit operational cost.

reviewCards.prompt: When does a case study's reasoning stop applying to you?
reviewCards.answer: When your constraints (team size, load, ownership) differ from the ones that drove their choice.
